author: Tim
title: Woman Wins $43 Million Jackpot But Casino Offers Steak Dinner
text:
Katrina Bookman thought her life had changed when the Sphinx slot machine at Resorts World Casino in Queens flashed a jackpot of $42,949,672.76. She snapped a selfie with the screen that read “printing cash ticket $42,949,672.76” because it felt like something you’d want proof of.
But she says things went south fast. According to her, casino staff escorted her out that same day and told her to come back tomorrow for an official answer.
Woman sues casino that offered her steak dinner instead of a $43 million jackpot https://t.co/9bX6mRqFMd pic.twitter.com/PcpqV9Bd4Q
— CNN (@CNN) June 17, 2017
When she asked what she won, she said they told her: “You didn’t win nothing.” Instead of millions, they offered her $2.25 and a steak dinner. So she took them to court.
Bookman filed a lawsuit at the Queens County Supreme Court against the casino and two companies involved with the machine. The complaint listed negligence, breach of contract, and misrepresentation.
Her lawyer Alan Ripka said: “You can’t claim a machine is broken because you want it to be broken.”
He asked: “Does that mean it wasn’t inspected? Does it mean it wasn’t maintained? And if so, does that mean that people that played there before [Bookman] had zero chance of winning?”
He also said: “The machine takes your money when you lose. It ought to pay it when you win.”
The casino didn’t agree. They said the payout was a clear error and blamed an “obvious malfunction.”
According to them, that type of machine isn’t even supposed to pay more than $6,500. They also pointed out that the machine includes a warning that says “Malfunctions void all pays and plays.”
But Ripka said: “The excuses given by the casino were ridiculous.” He claimed no one really explained how the machine broke or what actually happened.
The lawsuit also mentioned how hard this hit Bookman emotionally. She had grown up in foster care, was homeless for a while, and raised four kids on her own.
She told a local news station: “I kept thinking about my family. The struggle I’ve been through, it’s hard to cope.”
She had plans for that money. She wanted to open a barbershop for her son and do something good for her community. Instead, she said it left her feeling depressed and embarrassed.
Ripka argued that if she couldn’t get the full amount, she should at least be paid the $6,500 max prize the machine was supposed to allow.
But after delays from the pandemic, the court ended up siding with the casino. A judge ruled that the machine had malfunctioned and did show the message: “Malfunctions void all pays and plays.”
